chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Ibn Mahboub, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Aban ibn Taghlib, who said:
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'The believer is terrified in his sleep, so his sins are forgiven for him, and he is tested in his body, so his sins are forgiven for him.'
ai.seo_question: How do nightmares and illnesses serve as expiation for sins in Shia theology?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elucidates the mechanism of 'hastening punishment' (ta'jil al-'iqab) by identifying minor worldly afflictions—specifically fear during sleep and physical ailments—as expiatory means for a believer's sins. This reflects the Shia scholarly understanding that such trials are not punitive but merciful purifications, ensuring the soul is cleansed in this transient world rather than enduring greater retribution in the Hereafter. The narration underscores the spiritual significance of enduring daily hardships with patience as a direct path to divine forgiveness.

en.hubeali: A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Khalid, from Ibn Mahboub, from Hisham Bin Salim, from Aban Bin Taghlub who said,

‘Abu Abdullahasws said: ‘The Momin would be terrified upon (by a nightmare) in his sleep, so his sins would be Forgiven for him, and he would be Tested regarding his body (by an illness) so his sins would be Forgiven for him’.
en.sarwar: 4. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid from ibn Mahbub from Hisham ibn Salim from Aban ibn Taghlib who has said the following: “
Abu ‘Abd Allah (a.s.) has said, ‘A believer may suffer a nightmare so his sins are forgiven or is bodily humiliated so his sins are forgiven.’”
